raw_case_text:
A 11 weeks pregnant 24-year-old female sought medical attention for a 7-day progressive lower abdominal pain. She had no known medical condition with the exception of chlamydial cervicitis previously treated. She did not take any medications except for pregnancy related supplements and was an active smoker. Her current pregnancy was uneventful except for mild vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix assessed by ultrasound three weeks before presentation.
On admission, other than her abdominal pain, she denied bloating, diarrhea, or vomiting although close relatives who travelled with her did have diarrhea. The patient had recently travelled to the Caribbean and returned 7 days prior to presentation. During her trip she stayed in an all-inclusive resort. She denied any seafood consumption. She was found to be tachycardic and febrile at 39,3 C in the emergency room. Vaginal bleeding was initially similar to past bleeding episodes and did not orient clinicians toward an obstetrical infection. As such, Dengue and Zika virus serologies were ordered and returned negative in the next days. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level was 131,956 U/L on admission. A pelvic ultrasound revealed an intrauterine fetal pole with absent heart movement and a known stable anterior hematoma. Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam was administered with one dose of tobramycin and the patient spontaneously expelled product of conception and placenta in less than nine hours after triage in the emergency room. The patient progressed into a septic shock with transient vasopressors need; therefore she was brought to the operating room where dilatation and curettage was performed. Unfortunately, no material was found to be worth culturing at that time. Hemodynamic parameters improved promptly upon her return from the operating room. Four out of four blood culture bottles grew Gram-negative bacilli identified as Plesiomonas shigelloides by API 20NE (bioMerieux, Marcy L'Etoile, France) and confirmed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by Kirby-Bauer following CLSI M02-A12 method and interpreted according to CLSI M100S26 recommendations. The bacterium was resistant to ampicillin with intermediate resistance to cefazolin and gentamicin and was found to be susceptible to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amoxicillin-clavulanate, piperacillin-tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, TMP-SMX, tobramycin, and ertapenem. Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhea PCR on cervical swab were negative and, unfortunately, no bacterial cultures were realized. No stool specimen was obtained in the absence of GI symptoms. Neutrophil count peaked at 16.5 x 109/L during hospitalization, creatinine remained within the normal limits, and liver function tests were slightly elevated. She was discharged from the intensive care unit after 24 hours and control blood cultures were negative after 48 hours of antimicrobial therapy. She was then switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 3 of her admission and sent home on the fifth day to complete a 14-day course of antimicrobial therapy. On a follow-up visit five days after discharge, she was clinically well and her C-reactive protein was back to normal after reaching 256 mg/L on day two of her hospital stay.
Pathological analysis of the debris from the conceptus revealed chorioamnionitis, necrotizing deciduitis, and villitis. Gram stain on formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissue identified numerous Gram-negative bacilli within the chorionic villi and the placental membranes (Figure 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks of gestation presented with a 7-day history of progressive lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, an 11-week pregnant woman, presented to the emergency department with 7 days of progressively worsening lower abdominal pain and mild vaginal bleeding similar to a prior bleeding episode 3 weeks earlier (when ultrasound showed a closed cervix and stable anterior hematoma). She had returned 7 days prior to presentation from a vacation at an all-inclusive resort in the Caribbean, during which close traveling relatives experienced diarrhea, though the patient herself had no gastrointestinal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida at 11 weeks gestation; history of previously treated chlamydial cervicitis and mild first-trimester vaginal bleeding with a known anterior subchorionic hematoma 3 weeks prior. Active smoker. Travelled to an all-inclusive resort in the Caribbean, returning 7 days before admission; denied any seafood consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive lower abdominal pain, fever, and mild vaginal bleeding. Negative for abdominal bloating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Home medications: pregnancy-related supplements only.

objective.physical_examination: In the emergency department, the patient was febrile (39.3 C) and tachycardic, with mild vaginal bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) was 131,956 U/L. During hospitalization, neutrophil count peaked at 16.5 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) reached 256 mg/L on hospital day 2, liver function tests were slightly elevated, and serum creatinine remained within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound on admission demonstrated an intrauterine fetal pole with absent cardiac activity and a stable anterior hematoma.
objective.advanced_workup: Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion antimicrobial susceptibility testing (CLSI M02-A12 / M100S26) of the blood isolate showed resistance to ampicillin, intermediate resistance to cefazolin and gentamicin, and susceptibility to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amoxicillin-clavulanate, piperacillin-tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, tobramycin, and ertapenem. Histopathological examination of the expelled conceptus and placental tissues revealed acute chorioamnionitis, necrotizing deciduitis, and villitis, with Gram stain demonstrating numerous Gram-negative bacilli within the chorionic villi and placental membranes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Septic abortion and bacteremic chorioamnionitis caused by Plesiomonas shigelloides, complicated by transient septic shock. Four out of four blood culture bottles grew Gram-negative bacilli identified as Plesiomonas shigelloides by API 20NE and confirmed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Dengue and Zika virus serologies were negative, and cervical swab PCRs for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae were negative. Empiric intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and a single dose of tobramycin were initiated in the emergency department; she spontaneously expelled the products of conception within 9 hours, developed septic shock requiring transient vasopressor support, and underwent urgent surgical dilation and curettage in the operating room with rapid hemodynamic stabilization. She was discharged from the ICU after 24 hours, repeat blood cultures at 48 hours were sterile, and she was transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 3 and discharged home on day 5 to complete a 14-day antibiotic course. At 5-day post-discharge follow-up, she was clinically well with normalized CRP.
